analysis.one_liner: Blocks credit bureaus from reporting pandemic- and disaster-caused missed payments and COVID medical debt.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in March 2020, never got a committee vote in the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency and future federally declared major disasters, this bill would have stopped lenders and credit bureaus from reporting or including missed payments and other negative marks caused by the crisis. It would have banned reporting of medical debt from COVID or disaster treatment no matter when the bills were incurred, let consumers file a sworn hardship report to extend their protections, and required unlimited free credit reports and scores. It also barred credit scoring companies from rolling out new scoring models that would suddenly mark large numbers of people as less creditworthy.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary workers and households whose income was interrupted by the pandemic or a disaster. Their credit scores would be shielded from negative marks they could not avoid, COVID-related medical debt could never be used against them, and they could get free credit reports and scores whenever they needed them. People who later sought mortgages, apartments, car loans, or jobs that check credit would avoid paying higher interest or being denied because of pandemic-era marks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers hit by COVID or disasters

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits furnishing or including in credit reports any adverse information resulting from actions or inaction during the COVID-19 emergency period or a covered major disaster period (except felony convictions), for people in declared disaster areas [S3].
Bans reporting of medical debt related to COVID-19 or a major disaster treatment regardless of when the expenses were incurred [S3].

Requires the CFPB to set up a website where consumers can report economic hardship under penalty of perjury with no documentation required, extending credit protections an additional 270 days, and requires credit bureaus to automatically delete affected items [S3].
Requires credit bureaus to provide unlimited free credit reports and free credit scores during the emergency and for 12 months after, with online scores delivered within 15 minutes [S3].

Bars credit scoring companies from creating or implementing new scoring models during the emergency that would identify a significant percentage of consumers as less creditworthy than under the previous model [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies and the companies that furnish credit data lose their ability to report and profit from pandemic- and disaster-caused negative marks. Lenders and debt collectors lose negative credit reporting as leverage to collect from households that missed payments during the crisis.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, lenders, and debt collectors

drawbacks.text: The ban on requiring any documentation to substantiate hardship means some consumers who could have paid during the crisis would also get negative marks erased, and lenders would bear that unpriced risk [S3].

Suppressing accurate delinquency information during a crisis makes it harder for future lenders to price risk, which could reduce credit availability or raise rates for some borrowers after the protections expire [S3].
The bill carves out an exception for information related to felony criminal convictions, keeping that adverse information reportable even during a disaster [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection addresses a real, widespread harm: millions of people had their credit damaged through no fault of their own during a national emergency, and a credit ding follows a person into loans, housing, and employment for years. The cost falls on credit bureaus and lenders, whose legitimate objection is that a blanket no-documentation moratorium also shields some borrowers who could have paid and that suppressing data makes risk harder to price. Those are real design trade-offs, but they are modest compared with the scale of the harm the bill targets; the main reason it failed was not a debate about its merits, it was that it never received a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on March 23, 2020, three days after the national COVID emergency declaration, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1].
Fourteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all Democrats and none from the House's 197 Republicans [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further action after the referral; the bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus, lenders, and debt collectors kept their ability to report and profit from pandemic-caused negative marks; consumers got no protection and carry the resulting credit damage into loans and housing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus and lenders; consumers got nothing

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 23, 2020, to shield consumer credit from the effects of the COVID-19 outbreak and future disasters.

for.name: 14 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after its referral on March 23, 2020; the bill sat untouched until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill during its lifetime.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters (the sponsor plus 14 cosponsors) were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; but the bill never reached a vote, so no one ever had to go on record against it.

industries.industry: Consumer credit reporting agencies (Experian, Equifax, TransUnion, and specialty bureaus)
industries.note: Their business depends on collecting, scoring, and selling consumers' negative credit information, including missed payments and medical debt. The bill would have barred them from reporting or scoring most crisis-related negative marks, forced free unlimited reports and scores, and made them auto-delete flagged items.

Barred from deploying new scoring models during disasters that would significantly downgrade consumers relative to prior models, limiting their ability to tighten scoring during downturns. They also could not penalize consumers for information deleted under the bill's protections.

industries.industry: Lenders and furnishers of credit information
industries.note: They lose negative credit reporting as a collection tool for pandemic- and disaster-period delinquencies and absorb the resulting repayment risk, though their core lending business is otherwise untouched.

industries.industry: Medical debt collectors and medical billing collections
industries.note: The bill bans any credit reporting of medical debt arising from COVID-19 or major-disaster treatment regardless of when incurred, removing a major collection lever for unpaid medical bills.
